title: Token Economics & Tier Messaging: buyer-centric playbook
content:
Purpose
Purpose: give SDRs, AEs, PMs, and pricing owners a compact, high-utility playbook for: metric framing (why tokens), tier structure rationale, discounting guardrails, and quick competitive counters. Use this when drafting seatless proposals or prepping for pricing negotiations.

Audience
- Revenue (AEs, SDRs, Sales Eng)
- Product marketing / pricing
- Solutions engineers / CS for renewals

TL;DR (two-liners for quick copy)
- Why tokens: map price to actual usage so customers pay for what they ship, reduce surprise bills, and make economics explicit across features (chat, embeddings, reranking).
- Tiers: Design to align with buyer metric (dev adoption, production throughput, enterprise risk). Give clear commit incentives: deeper discounts for time-bound committed tokens and multi-region SLAs.

Core messaging pillars (short bullets to reuse)
1) Usage-aligned fairness: Tokens let teams correlate cost directly with value delivered (requests, embeddings, tokens generated) — better ROI visibility than seat or per-model vans.
2) Predictable economics: Commits + token pools convert variable usage into predictable unit economics while preserving scale flexibility.
3) Performance parity across modes: Same token currency across hosted, dedicated, and private — one accounting layer for ops and finance.
4) Operational controls: Budgets, per-route throttles, and token forecasting reduce surprise overages.

Metric-framing: translate technical metrics into buyer language
- Developer / Platform lead: "Tokens let us measure and forecast monthly usage per endpoint and correlate to product launches" -> emphasize fast experiment-to-prod and predictable unit cost.
- Product manager (feature ROI): Tie tokens per active-user feature to revenue uplift tests; show token-per-DIU (daily interacting user) estimates.
- Infra / SRE: Map tokens to GPU-hours and tail-latency budgets; explain commit sizing reduces burst risk and improves capacity guarantees for Dedicated.
- Procurement / Finance: Show token consumption models across scenarios (conservative / expected / aggressive) and equivalent dollar spend; highlight committed discounts and renewal step-downs.

Why token pricing? (talking points + metaphors)
- Analogy: tokens are to LLMs what compute hours were to cloud VMs — metric tied to consumption, flexible across instance types.
- Key benefits: granular visibility, decouples price from headcount (no per-seat friction), supports mixed workloads (short chat vs long generation vs embeddings) under one unit.
- Risk mitigation: token pools + alerting = no bill shock; rolling forecasts and auto-top-ups available.

When tokens are NOT ideal (acknowledge limits)
- Small teams wanting a blunt monthly price with no metering (offer a small fixed monthly package).
- Customers who demand per-user metrics for internal chargeback (we can provide per-route consumption dashboards that map tokens to users).

Tier design rationale (narrative + examples)
Goal: map tiers to buyer journeys and commit-intensity, not just raw token counts. Keep 4 tiers: Trial, Growth, Business, Enterprise.
- Trial: free tier with starter token credit (e.g., 200k tokens) + API keys, basic telemetry. Purpose: low friction eval and embedding experiments.
- Growth: pay-as-you-go with volume breaks and starter committed pool option (monthly tokens, modest discount). Targets: dev teams and early PLG motion.
- Business: for productizing features -> mid-size committed pools (quarterly or annual), feature flags (dedicated routing, higher retention), SLO credits.
- Enterprise: large commits, multi-region SLAs, private deploy options, custom audit/KMS, on-prem connectors and white-glove onboarding. Pricing: highest discounts for multi-year/volume/capacity reservation.

Discounting language & guardrails (sales playbook)
Principles:
- Default is list price; discounts are tied to commitments (term length, token volume, add-on services).
- Avoid ad-hoc % for convenience; anchor discount to a named program: e.g., "Commit Discount" or "Capacity Reservation Credit".
- Protect unit economics: define minimum unit price by tier; discounts must not drop below that floor.

Typical discount bands (guideline, internal only)
- Small commit (monthly, <10k USD): 0–5% (or none)
- Standard commit (annual, mid-size): 10–20%
- Large strategic commit (multi-year, large volume + private): 20–40%
- Additive for prepayment: +2–5% for upfront payment
- Implementation services / migration credits are separate line items, not part of token discounting.

Negotiation scripts (sample language)
- If customer asks for a flat % reduction: "We can wrap that into a Commit Discount — tell me the horizon you want to commit and we’ll map to the right program so you get billing predictability and a pricing break that scales with consumption."
- If procurement asks to move to per-seat: "We can provide per-user chargeback views, but tokens align cost directly with user activity and ensure you don’t pay for dormant seats."
- If concerned about bill shock: "We’ll set a soft cap, push alerts, and create a monthly forecast with you. You can choose to auto-top-up or stay within the committed pool."

Competitive analysis notes (how to counter common alternatives)
- Per-request pricing (competitor): sells simplicity but punishes heavy outputs. Counter: tokens more accurately capture cost variance by output length and model type.
- Per-seat pricing: simple for orgs with steady users but poor for public-facing products. Counter: tokens avoid paying for unused seats and scale with usage spikes.
- Flat model-specific pricing: can be cheaper for some patterns but lacks cross-model portability and makes model upgrades/broad use harder. Counter: tokens work across model variants and deployment modes; routing policies preserve cost controls.

Common objections & short rebuttals
- "We don’t want complexity": "We provide guardrails and default presets (monthly commit templates) so most customers never touch the knobs."
- "How do we forecast?": "Template scenarios + per-route historical metrics -> 3-point forecast (conservative/expected/aggressive) we share during the POC."
- "Tokens feel abstract": "We translate tokens into example calls (e.g., X tokens ≈ 1k chat messages at 80 tokens/msg) and provide a usage simulator in the console."

Examples & worked scenarios (one-pagers to reuse)
- Embeddings-heavy app: show tokens per embedding vector, batch sizing recommendations, projected cost per 10k vectors, compare commit vs PAYG.
- Chat assistant with long context: show average tokens per session, tail sensitivity, recommended commit levels to keep 95th percentile latency within SLOs.

Sales enablement snippets (copyable)
- Email opener: "We price by token so you only pay for what your app generates — commits get you discounts and predictable cost, while pay-as-you-go keeps it simple for early experiments."
- Demo line: "Let me show live how a single query maps to tokens and how the console forecasts month-end spend."

Portal / console features to highlight
- Per-route token dashboards, forecast simulator, commit vs usage visual, alerting/soft caps, token transfer between projects (governance controls).

Implementation notes for PM/engineers (short)
- Billing counter: Tokens should be recorded per model-call with labels for model, route, project, and org. Keep event-level logs for 90 days and aggregated metrics for 13 months.
- Export: CSV/BI connector for finance reconciliation. Provide a "token-to-dollar" monthly summary line for procurement.

Open questions & TODOs
- Define the minimum unit price floor per tier (finance + product to finalize).
- Build a simple usage simulator widget for the console (SE asks).
- Draft 1-pager for procurement that maps token scenarios to CapEx/Opex expectations.
- Finalize the public-facing discount bands and legal wording for SOWs.

Appendix: sample visuals to create (descriptions only)
- "3-scenario forecast" chart: conservative/expected/aggressive token consumption over 12 months.
- "Token anatomy" infographic: show how chat + embeddings convert into tokens and where batching helps.
- "Commit decision tree": asks to guide sales through commit size & term recommendations.

Notes to reviewer
- Please flag any competitive cases we missed (notable vendors using seat or flat-model pricing).
- Prioritize creation of the console simulator; SEs report it short-circuits most pricing objections.

End.
